title: Conditional Access
summary: Conditional access is a policy engine that evaluates signals about a sign-in attempt and then decides whether to allow it, block it, or allow it only after additional requirements are satisfied such as multi-factor authentication, a compliant device or a trusted network location. The signals typically include user or group membership, application being accessed, device platform, device compliance or join state, client application type, source IP address and named location, and sign-in risk or user risk computed by the identity provider. This is the mechanism that turns identity from a binary decision into a graded one, and it is the practical enforcement point for zero trust principles in most enterprise estates today because it can require stronger evidence for sensitive applications while keeping low-risk access frictionless. The security outcome depends entirely on policy coverage and on how exceptions are managed: a policy that excludes a service account, a legacy protocol client or a break-glass identity creates a path that does not require the control, and adversaries deliberately hunt for those paths by attempting authentication through older client stacks that cannot satisfy modern requirements. Policy design therefore needs both a default posture that blocks what is not explicitly permitted and a deliberate, documented set of exclusions with compensating monitoring. Orchestration between policies matters too, since many platforms combine all applicable policies and require satisfaction of every grant control they contain, so an apparently narrow policy can change behaviour for a large population. Defenders rely on the resulting telemetry, because sign-in logs annotated with policy outcomes allow alerting on repeated policy failures from one identity, on successful sign-ins that bypassed an expected control, and on new or modified policy definitions that quietly weaken posture.
objectives: You will be able to enumerate the signals available to a conditional access policy and select the ones relevant to a stated requirement.
You will be able to distinguish grant controls from session controls and explain how multiple applicable policies combine.
You will be able to design a policy set with a blocking default and documented, monitored exclusions.
You will be able to identify bypass paths created by legacy authentication clients, service accounts and break-glass identities.
You will be able to detect policy weakening by monitoring changes to policy definitions alongside sign-in outcomes.
You will be able to troubleshoot a user access failure by reading policy evaluation results in the sign-in log.
